items.question: How do you think AI capabilities will continue to improve from here?
items.object: Sources of future AI capability growth
items.answer: Multiple vectors of progress. So, I think there is probably a little bit more juice out of the scalability lemon to be squeezed. So, hopefully we continue to make progress there, but it's getting really, really difficult. Society's perception of AI has been very skewed by the PR machinery of a handful of companies with amazing PR capabilities. Because that number of companies drove scale, the narrative people think of is scale first as a vector of progress. But I think agentic workflows, the way we built multimodal models, we did a lot of work to build concrete applications. There are multiple vectors of progress, as well as wild cards like brand new technologies, like can diffusion models, which are used to generate images for the most part, also work for generating text? I think that's exciting. So, I think there'll be multiple ways for AI to make progress.

I think that's exciting. So, I think there'll be multiple ways for AI to make progress.

items.question: Why did you choose to introduce the term “agentic AI”?
items.object: Agentic AI as a way to describe degrees of agency
items.answer: So when I decided to start talking about agentic AI, which wasn't a thing when I started to use the term, my team was slightly annoyed at me. One of my team members, that I won't name, said, “Andrew, the world does not need you to make up another term.” But I decided to do it anyway, and for whatever reason, it stuck. The reason I started to talk about agentic AI was because a couple years ago I saw people would spend a lot of time debating, “Is this an agent? Is this not an agent? What is an agent?” I felt there's a lot of good work, and there was a spectrum of degrees of agency, where there are highly autonomous agents that could plan, take multiple sets of reasoning, do a lot of stuff by themselves, and then things that were lower degrees of agency, where you would prompt an alarming output. I felt like, rather than debating, “Is this an agent or not?” let's just say the degrees of agency and say it's all agentic, so we spend our time actually building this. So I started to push the term agentic AI.

One of my team members, that I won't name, said, “Andrew, the world does not need you to make up another term.” But I decided to do it anyway, and for whatever reason, it stuck.

items.question: How do you assess the enthusiasm around agentic AI relative to its actual business progress?
items.object: Marketing hype and business progress around agentic AI
items.answer: What I did not expect was that several months later a bunch of marketers would get ahold of this term and use it as a sticker to stick it on everything in sight. And so I think the term agentic AI really took off. I feel like the marketing hype has gone insanely fast, but the real business progress has also been rapidly growing, but maybe not as fast as the marketing.

items.question: How do you see the prospects for automating the engineering work needed to build AI agent workflows?
items.object: Automating the engineering work required to build AI agent workflows
items.answer: It turns out that a lot of this process of building agent workflows requires ingesting external knowledge, which is often locked up in the heads of people. So until and unless we build AI avatars that can interview employees doing the work and better visual AI that can look at the computer monitor, maybe eventually. But I think at least right now, for the next year or two, there's a lot of work for human engineers to do to build more agent workflows. That's more the kind of collection of data, feedback, etc. for certain loops that people are doing.

items.question: Why do you see human judgment as necessary when implementing multi-step agent workflows for business processes?
items.object: Human judgment in implementing multi-step agent workflows
items.answer: I see a lot of workflows like maybe a customer emails your document. You got to convert the document to text and maybe do a web search for some compliance reason to see if you're working with a vendor you're not supposed to, and then look up a database record, see the pricing, save it somewhere else, and so on. Multi-step, multi-region workflows, kind of next-gen robotic process automation. So you implement this and it doesn't work. Is it a problem if you got the invoice date wrong? Is that a problem or not? Or if you routed a message to the wrong person for verification? When you implement these things, almost always it doesn't work the first time. But then, to know what's important for your business process, is it okay that I bothered the CEO of the company too many times, or the CEO doesn't mind verifying some invoices? All that external contextual knowledge, at least right now, I see thoughtful human product managers or human engineers having to think through and make these decisions. So can an agent do that someday? I don't know. Seems pretty difficult right now. Maybe someday.

items.question: What makes AI coding agents stand out to you at the frontier of agentic AI?
items.object: AI coding agents as examples of autonomous agentic AI
items.answer: I feel like at the bleeding edge of agentic AI, I've been really impressed by some of the AI coding agents. So I think in terms of economic value, there are two very clear and very apparent buckets. One is answering people's questions. OpenAI ChatGPT seems to be the market leader in that, with real growth takeoff, liftoff velocity. The second massive bucket of economic value is coding agents. My personal favorite right now is Claude Code. Maybe it will change at some point, but I just use it, love it. Highly autonomous in terms of planning out what to do to build the software, building a checklist, going through it one at a time. So this ability to plan a multi-step thing, execute the multiple steps of a plan, is one of the most highly autonomous things out there being used that actually works. There's other stuff that I think doesn't work, like some of the computer-use stuff, like “go shop for something for me and browse online.” Some of those things are really nice demos, but not yet production.

items.question: What excites you about AI models helping develop the next generation of models?
items.object: AI models helping develop the next generation of models
items.answer: So I feel like we're slowly getting there. Some of the leading foundation model companies are clearly—well, they've said publicly they're using AI to write a lot of the code. Maybe one thing I find exciting is AI models using agentic workflows to generate data for the next generation of models. I think the Llama research paper talked about this, but an older version of Llama would be used to think for a long time to generate puzzles that then you train the next generation of the model to try to solve really quickly without needing to think as long. So I find that exciting too. Multiple vectors of progress. It feels like AI is not just one way to make progress. There's so many smart people pushing forward in so many different ways.

items.question: How do you assess the potential of AI tools to accelerate product management?
items.object: AI tools for accelerating product management
items.answer: Yeah, so there's been a bunch of tools to try to speed up product management. The recent Figma IPO is one great example of design AI. Heidi and Dylan did a great job. Then there are these tools that are trying to use AI to help interview prospective users, and as you say, we looked at some of the scientific papers on using a flock of AI agents to simulate a group of users and how to calibrate that. It all feels promising and early, and hopefully wildly exciting in the future. I don't think those tools are accelerating product managers nearly as much as coding tools are accelerating software engineers. So this does create more of the bottleneck on the product management side. It does make sense to me that my partner Mike has this idea that I think is broadly applicable in a couple different ways: computers can now interrogate humans at scale. And so there's companies like Lucen Labs working on this for consumer research-type tasks, right? But you could also use it to understand tasks for training or the data collection piece.

items.question: What qualities do you think make a startup founder more likely to succeed as generative AI advances?
items.object: Founder capabilities and company strategy amid rapid generative AI progress
items.answer: To me, there are so many things that the world used to do in 2022 that just do not work in 2025. In fact, often I ask myself, is there anything we're doing today that we're also doing in 2022? And if so, let's take a look and see if it still even makes sense today, because a lot of stuff, a lot of workflows in 2020 don't make sense today. I think today the technology is moving so fast. Founders that are on top of gen AI technology, tech-oriented product leaders, I think are much more likely to succeed than someone that maybe is more business-oriented, more business-savvy, but doesn't have a good feel for where AI is going. I think unless you have a good feel for what this technology can do, it's really difficult to think about strategy and where to lead the company.

items.answer: You know, I work very hard. There are periods in my life where I encourage others that want to have a great career of impact, like, work hard. items.question: Why do you believe startups are not for everyone?
items.object: The work ethic and conviction required to build a startup
items.answer: I'd say something maybe a little less politically correct: I think there was an era where people thought there was a statement that startups are for everyone, and I do not believe that's true. You're trying to do a very unreasonable thing, which is create a lot of value, impacting people very quickly. When you're trying to do an unreasonable thing, you probably have to work pretty hard. I think the work ethic required to move the needle in the world very quickly disappeared. There was a quote—I wish I remembered who said this—but was it, “The only people that would change the world are the ones crazy enough to think they can”? I think it does take someone with the bonus, the decisiveness to go and say, “You know what? Just save the world. I'm going to take a shot at changing it.” It's only people with that conviction that I think can do this.

items.question: Why do you think leaders who succeeded in an earlier generation of companies can struggle when they join scaling AI companies?
items.object: Leadership effectiveness in rapidly changing AI companies
items.answer: The other thing that I've observed is just the floor is lava, right? The ground is changing in terms of capability all the time, and the competition is also very fierce in the categories that are already obviously important and have multiple players. Leaders who are really effective in companies a generation ago are not necessarily that effective when recruited into these companies as they're scaling, because of the pace of the velocity of operation or the pace of change. It's interesting to see you say, “I'm looking at what I was doing today and in 2022 and saying, is that still right?” If you're an engineering leader or a go-to-market leader and you've built your career being really great at how that's done, that may not be applicable anymore. I think it's a challenge for a lot of people. I know many great leaders in lots of different functions still doing things the way they were in 2022. It has got to change when new technology comes.

items.question: Why do you see effective AI use and learning to code as important for people in non-engineering roles?
items.object: AI fluency and coding skills in non-engineering jobs
items.answer: Once upon a time there was no such thing as web search. Today, who would you hire for any role that doesn't know how to search the web? I think we're well past the point that for a lot of job roles, if you can't use AI in an effective way, you're much less effective than someone that can. Everyone in my team at AI Fund knows how to code. I see for a lot of my team members, when my assistant general counsel or my CFO or my front desk operator learns how to code, they're not software engineers, but they do their job function better because by learning the language of computers, they can now tell a computer more precisely what they want it to do for them, and the computer does it for them. This makes them more effective at their job function. I think the rapid pace of change is disconcerting to a lot of people.

items.question: What do you find revealing about how early adopters of Harvey, the legal AI company, are thinking about the future of their businesses?
items.object: AI-driven transformation of legal work and other industries
items.answer: When I led Harvey's Series B, I called a bunch of their customers, and the thing that was most interesting to me about some of those customer calls was, because legal is notorious as being a tough profession for adopting new technology, there aren't a dozen great legal software companies. Those customers that I called, which were big law firms or people who were quite far along in terms of adopting Harvey, all thought this was the future. They all thought that AI was really going to matter for their vertical, and the main thing they would raise questions about was, “In a world where this is ubiquitous, suddenly instead of hiring 100 associates I only hire 10, and how do I think about future partners and who to promote if I don't have a big pool?” I thought that mindset shift was really interesting. I feel like it's percolating into all these markets or industries. It's slowly happening, and as industry by industry people are starting to rethink aspects of their business in really interesting ways. It'll take a decade, two decades for this transformation to happen, but it's compelling to see how the earliest-adopting verticals and the people thinking deepest about it should be really interesting.
quotes: One company that I guess both of us are involved with is called Harvey, and I led their Series B.

When I did that, I called a bunch of their customers, and the thing that was most interesting to me about some of those customer calls was, because legal is notorious as being a tough profession for adopting new technology, there aren't a dozen great legal software companies.

Those customers that I called, which were big law firms or people who were quite far along in terms of adopting Harvey, all thought this was the future. They all thought that AI was really going to matter for their vertical, and the main thing they would raise questions about was, “In a world where this is ubiquitous, suddenly instead of hiring 100 associates I only hire 10, and how do I think about future partners and who to promote if I don't have a big pool?”

I thought that mindset shift was really interesting, and to your point, I feel like it's percolating into all these markets or industries. It's slowly happening, and as industry by industry people are starting to rethink aspects of their business in really interesting ways. It'll take a decade, two decades for this transformation to happen, but it's compelling to see how the earliest-adopting verticals and the people thinking deepest about it should be really interesting.

items.question: How do you judge whether keeping a startup small and profitable is holding back its growth?
items.object: Capital efficiency versus growth in startups
items.answer: For me, it's basically, are you being lackadaisical or too accepting of the progress that your company's making because it's going just fine? It could be going much better, but it's still going great on a relative basis. And so you're like, “Oh, I'll keep the team small. I'll be super lean. I won't spend any money. Look at me, how profitable I am.” Sometimes that's amazing; capital efficiency is great. But sometimes you're actually missing the opportunity or not going as fast as you can. Usually what happens is in the early stage of a startup's life, you're competing with other startups, and if you're way ahead it feels great. But eventually, if there are incumbents in your market, they come in, and the faster you capture the market and move up market, the less time you give them to realize what's going on and catch on. Often five, six, seven years into the life of a startup, you're actually competing with incumbents suddenly, and they just kill you with distribution or other things. People really miss the mark, and you could argue that was kind of Slack versus Teams. There are a few companies I won't name, but I feel like they're so proud of their profitability and they kind of blew up, I guess, on the design side. That was Sketch, right? Remember Bohemian Coding?

items.question: How do you understand the efficiency of small teams using AI?
items.object: Small-team efficiency with AI and staffing at big tech companies

items.question: Why do you think an instinct for using AI matters when deciding how to resource a team's work?
items.object: AI instinct in team resourcing
items.answer: I feel like this is another reason why that AI instinct is so important. I remember one week I had two conversations with two different team members. One person came to me to say, “Hey, Andrew, I want to do this. Can you give me some more headcount to do this?” I said no. Later that week, independently, someone else said, “Hey, Andrew, can you give me some budget to hire AI to do this?” I said yes. That realization: you hire AI, not a lot more humans for this. You just got to have those instincts.

items.question: Why do you prefer concrete startup ideas when deciding what to build at AI Fund?
items.object: Concrete startup ideas at AI Fund
items.answer: If someone—a subject matter expert or an engineer—comes and says, “I have an idea. Look at this part of healthcare operations and drive all this,” they go, “Okay, great.” That's a concrete idea. I don't know if it's a good idea or a bad idea, but it's concrete; at least we could very efficiently figure out, do customers want this? Is this technically feasible? And get going. I find that at AI Fund, when we're trying to decide what to build, we spin a long list of ideas to try to select a small number that we want to go forward on. We don't like looking at ideas that are not concrete.

items.question: Why do you think relationship advantages in company building are hard to fully automate?
items.object: Relationship advantages in company building
items.answer: The other thing I think is very durable is things that rely on a relationship advantage. If I'm convincing somebody to work at one of my companies and they worked at a previous company and they trust me because of it, or whatever reason, all the information in the world about why this is a good opportunity isn't the same thing as me being like, “Sally, you got to do this. It's going to work.” It remains to be seen whether or not company building is actually that correlated with investment returns, but I do think that side of it feels harder to fully automate.

items.question: How do you think about setting highly technical first-time founders up for success?
items.object: Supporting highly technical first-time founders
items.answer: We increasingly see highly technical people try to be first-time founders. How do you set up the processes for first-time founders to learn all the hard lessons and all the craziness needed to be a successful founder? I spent a lot of time thinking through that: how to set up founders for success when they have 80% of the skills needed to be really great, but there's another little bit that we can help them with.

items.question: How do you think about helping first-time founders who have most of the skills they need but still have gaps?
items.object: Helping first-time founders develop missing skills
items.answer: I just view it as a mix of peer groups: can you surround people with other people who are either similar or one or two steps ahead of them on the founding journey? And then the second thing is complementary hire. One of my big learnings is, early in careers people try to build out the skills that they don't have. Later in careers, they lean into what they're really good at and hire people to do the rest. If the company's working, I think you just hire people. Bill Gates would notoriously talk about his COO being the person he'd learned the most from, and then once he had a certain level of scale, he'd hire his next COO.
